events/1300_priore/phases/0/transitionTe: At the lectern, Boccaccio writes down a year: 1300.
events/1300_priore/phases/0/announcement: Boccaccio: “Remember this year. In real life, this is the year he became a prior. And he set the story of the Divine Comedy in this year too — the middle of a life. Why? Listen, and you will see.”
events/1300_priore/phases/1/travelNarrat: Pope Boniface VIII invents the “Jubilee”: anyone who comes to Rome as a pilgrim this year has every sin forgiven. Two hundred thousand people pour into Rome — Dante among them.
events/1300_priore/phases/1/instruction: Click each stop along the route.
events/1300_priore/phases/1/waypoints/0/: The whole city is packing. To Rome! To the Jubilee!
events/1300_priore/phases/1/waypoints/1/: The old road never empties: pilgrims, peddlers, beggars, a lady's litter. Every language is saying the same word — Rome.
events/1300_priore/phases/1/waypoints/2/: Inside the gates and out, people swarm like ants. On the bridge the crowd is split into two lines going opposite ways, so nobody gets trampled.
Like an army crossing a bridge, in two lines… I am keeping this picture.
events/1300_priore/phases/2/narrative: Rome. Two hundred thousand pilgrims turn the streets into rivers.
events/1300_priore/phases/2/instruction: Click the people and things in the scene.
events/1300_priore/phases/2/npcs/0/dialo: Guards keeping order have split the bridge down the middle: one side for those going to St Peter's, the other for those coming back.
Years later I wrote the ditches of Hell's eighth circle: the sinners walk in two lines, opposite ways — “just like the crowd on the bridge in Rome in the Jubilee year.”
events/1300_priore/phases/2/npcs/1/dialo: Hymns in every accent, all mixed together. Some have come the whole way on their knees, and their knees are raw.
events/1300_priore/phases/2/npcs/2/name: The money chest by the altar
events/1300_priore/phases/2/npcs/2/dialo: By the altar, priests rake a mountain of offerings into the chest with long rakes, day and night.
Forgiveness and gold coin, traded across the same altar.
events/1300_priore/phases/3/transitionTe:
Outside St Peter's. Far off on a high platform, a figure in a gold crown takes the cheers of two hundred thousand people.
No conversation. Only power, pressing down.
events/1300_priore/phases/3/announcement: Boniface VIII: “Whoever comes devoutly to the tomb of the Apostle in this holy year shall have every sin forgiven.”
events/1300_priore/phases/3/dufu_reactio: He has taken the keys of Heaven and cast them into a sceptre for this world. Remember this man — Boniface.
events/1300_priore/phases/4/petitions/0/: “You'd drive us out too? We're your own party.”
“Then I'll go to the pope myself.”
events/1300_priore/phases/4/petitions/1/: Leave me out of it. I'm your best friend.
events/1300_priore/phases/4/petitions/2/: Exile both sides together. That is the only way the rule holds.
“Why are we counted in as well?”
“Then what have we been doing these two months?”
events/1300_priore/phases/4/closing: However you choose, someone is unhappy.
events/1300_priore/phases/5/title: Your Closest Friend Is On the List
events/1300_priore/phases/5/narrative: The pen hangs over the list. Under ringleaders of the Whites: Guido Cavalcanti — the man who taught you to write poetry, your “first friend.”
events/1300_priore/phases/5/options/0/re: Then the order against the Blacks is void too — Corso stays in the city, and the blood on the Santa Trinita square was spilled for nothing. The city goes up in flames.
events/1300_priore/phases/5/options/1/te: Sign. The same rule for everyone.
events/1300_priore/phases/5/options/1/re:
(quietly) Guido, forgive me.
The city comes before the man.
events/1300_priore/phases/5/conclusion/n: Cavalcanti was sent to Sarzana, where the swamp air was full of fever. He caught malaria; he was allowed home, and died that August. Years later, in Inferno X, Dante meets his father — the old man sits up out of a burning tomb: “Where is my son? Why is he not walking with you?” Dante hesitates for one moment, and the old man, thinking his son is dead, falls back into the tomb. Dante never got to finish the sentence.
events/1300_priore/phases/6/panels/0/dia: Dante the prior, bent over his desk. The candle flame wavers.
events/1300_priore/phases/6/panels/1/dia: The picture darkens. The papers on the desk slowly turn into vines and branches.
events/1300_priore/phases/6/panels/2/dia: Years later he picks up the pen and sets the story back in this year — the middle of his life, the year when nothing was lost yet and everything had already begun to go.

Nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita —
Midway on the journey of our life, I found myself in a dark wood, for the right road was lost.
events/1300_priore/phases/7/prompt:
The first line of the Comedy is a man lost in a wood.
Use the pieces below to build one sentence: why does he start the book here?
events/1300_priore/phases/7/sentence: Because {s1}, {s2} — {s3}. So he made the first page of the book {s4}.
events/1300_priore/phases/7/tokens/0/tex: the city was torn in two by the two parties
events/1300_priore/phases/7/tokens/1/tex: he became a prior and, by the rule, exiled the leading men of both parties together
events/1300_priore/phases/7/tokens/2/tex: his close friend Guido was on the list and he signed anyway; Guido fell ill in exile and died soon after coming home
events/1300_priore/phases/7/tokens/3/tex: a man in a dark wood who cannot find the right road
events/1300_priore/phases/7/tokens/4/tex: he saw the pope in Rome in the Jubilee year
events/1300_priore/phases/7/tokens/5/tex: Florence's florin coin was used all over Europe
events/1300_priore/phases/7/canonical: Because the city was torn in two by the two parties, he became a prior and by the rule exiled the leading men of both parties together — his close friend Guido was on the list and he signed anyway; Guido fell ill in exile and died soon after coming home. So he made the first page of the book a man in a dark wood who cannot find the right road.
events/1300_priore/phases/7/note:
Two pieces are left over: the pope and the coin are both real, and both matter, but they are not on this chain of cause and effect.

“Lost” is not a figure of speech. He did the public thing right and destroyed his friend; two years later the same rule was used to destroy him. A man has to get that far before he says he is in the middle of a wood and cannot find the road.
events/1300_priore/phases/8/transitionTe:
There is light on the hilltop. Three beasts block the road.
This is page one of the Comedy — and what it describes is himself, in 1300.
events/1300_priore/phases/8/announcement: Boccaccio: “In the real 1300 he signed his closest friend onto an exile list. In the invented 1300 he is lost in a dark wood. My friends — these two are the same thing.”
quiz/1300_priore/quizzes/0/question: In which year did Dante set the story of the Divine Comedy?
quiz/1300_priore/quizzes/0/options/1: 1300 (the year he was a prior, the middle of his life)
quiz/1300_priore/quizzes/0/explanation: The Comedy is set in Easter week, 1300 — “midway on the journey of our life,” age thirty-five. That is exactly the year he became a prior in real life, the year everything was about to turn: nothing lost yet, and everything already beginning to go.
quiz/1300_priore/quizzes/1/question: In 1300, while Dante was a prior, which close friend did he exile to stop the party fighting?
quiz/1300_priore/quizzes/1/explanation: To stop the Whites and Blacks killing each other, and to keep “the same rule for everyone,” the priors exiled the ringleaders of both parties together — and on the Whites' list was Cavalcanti, Dante's “first friend.” He caught malaria in the fever country and died that August. Corso was the leader of the Blacks who was exiled.
quiz/1300_priore/quizzes/2/question:
Fill in the opening of the Inferno:
“Midway on the journey of our life, I found myself in a ___ wood”
quiz/1300_priore/quizzes/2/explanation: The opening of Inferno I: “Nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita / mi ritrovai per una selva oscura” — Midway on the journey of our life, I found myself in a dark wood.
